Communism is a political and economic system built on one central belief: that society works best when everything is owned collectively by the people as a whole, rather than by private individuals. In a fully communist society, there is no private property (in the economic sense), no social classes, and no government as we know it — and resources are shared based on what each person needs.

The guiding principle of communism is summed up in a famous phrase: "From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs." This means everyone contributes what they can, and everyone receives what they require to live well — regardless of how much they individually produced.
The Problem Communism Claims to Solve

To understand communism, you first need to understand what it was reacting against.

In a capitalist society, some people own businesses, factories, and land — these are called the means of production. Workers, who don't own these things, must sell their labor to the owners in exchange for wages. Communist thinkers argued this arrangement is fundamentally unfair, because the owner profits from the worker's labor without doing the actual work. The owner gets richer; the worker stays poor. Over time, wealth concentrates in fewer and fewer hands, while the majority struggles.

Communists called this exploitation — and they believed it was not an accident or a result of individual greed, but a built-in feature of capitalism itself.
Where Communism Comes From

The most influential architects of communist thought were Karl Marx (a German philosopher) and Friedrich Engels (his collaborator), who laid out their ideas in the 19th century. Their most famous work, The Communist Manifesto (1848), argued that all of human history is essentially a story of class struggle — the powerful exploiting the powerless. They saw capitalism as just the latest version of this struggle (owners vs. workers), and believed it would eventually collapse under its own contradictions, giving way to a new, fairer system.

Marx developed these ideas further in his massive work Das Kapital, where he analyzed how capitalism extracts value from workers and why he believed it was destined to fail.
How Communism Is Supposed to Work (In Theory)

Marx and later thinkers described a rough progression of stages that society would pass through:

1. Capitalism — The starting point. Owners dominate workers; wealth is concentrated; inequality is severe.

2. Revolution — Workers, fed up with exploitation, rise up and overthrow the capitalist class. This is seen as inevitable, because workers vastly outnumber owners.

3. Socialism — A transitional phase. The state (now controlled by the working class) takes ownership of the means of production. Wealth is redistributed more fairly, but some government control is still necessary during this phase to manage the transition.

4. Full Communism — The final stage. Because there are no more classes and no more exploitation, the state is no longer needed and simply "withers away." Society organizes itself, resources are shared freely, and no one is exploited.

It's important to note that full communism was always seen as a distant goal, not something that could be built overnight. The societies that called themselves communist (like the Soviet Union or China) were officially claiming to be in the socialist transitional stage — moving toward communism — not that they had achieved it.
Key Features of a Communist Society (The Ideal)

• No private ownership of the means of production. Factories, farms, mines, and major businesses belong to the community collectively — not to individuals. (Personal belongings like your clothes or furniture are a different matter.)
  • No social classes. There is no "rich class" and no "poor class." Everyone stands on equal footing economically.
  • No state. In the full communist vision, the government eventually disappears because it was only ever needed to manage class conflict — and once classes no longer exist, neither does the need for a coercive state.
  • Distribution by need. You don't earn money for your labor and then buy things. Instead, society produces what is needed and distributes it based on what individuals actually need to live.
  • Collective planning. Instead of the market deciding what gets produced (as in capitalism), the community collectively plans production to serve human needs rather than profit.
Communism in Practice: What Actually Happened

The 20th century saw several countries attempt to build communist (or socialist-transitional) states. The most significant examples are:

  • Soviet Union (USSR), 1917–1991 — The first major communist state, born out of the Russian Revolution led by Vladimir Lenin. The government took control of all major industries and farms, abolished private ownership of productive assets, and created a centrally planned economy. Under Joseph Stalin, it industrialized rapidly but at enormous human cost — millions died from famine, forced labor, and political repression.
  • China (People's Republic of China), 1949–present — Led by Mao Zedong, China became a communist state. It followed a similar path of collective ownership and state planning, but since the 1980s has introduced significant elements of capitalism into its economy while the Communist Party retains total political power.
  • Cuba, 1959–present — Fidel Castro established a communist government after a revolution. Cuba nationalized industries, provided free healthcare and education to all citizens, but also severely restricted political freedoms.
  • North Korea, 1948–present — Officially a socialist state, it is among the most isolated and authoritarian regimes in the world, using the name of communism to justify one-family rule.

In virtually every case, the pattern was similar: the state never "withered away" as Marx predicted. Instead, it grew more powerful. Central planning proved difficult to execute efficiently. Political opposition was crushed. And the gap between the ideal of communism and the reality of these regimes became one of the most significant political stories of the 20th century.
Why Communism and Socialism Are Different (But Related)

People often confuse the two, so this is worth clarifying directly.

Socialism is a broader idea that simply means the community (or the state) owns and manages major industries and resources, rather than private individuals. It does not necessarily mean eliminating all classes or having no government. Many democratic countries have significant socialist elements (like public healthcare or nationalized railways) while still operating as market economies.

Communism is more radical. It goes beyond socialism to demand the complete abolition of private property, social classes, and the state itself. Socialism can coexist with democracy and markets. Communism, as an ideology, envisions a total transformation of society.

In Marxist theory, socialism is the step before communism — a transitional phase. But in everyday political usage, the two words are often used loosely and sometimes interchangeably, which creates a lot of confusion.
Why Communism Has Been Criticized

Communism has attracted serious, well-founded criticism from multiple directions:

On efficiency: Central planning — where the government decides what to produce, in what quantities, and at what price — has proven very difficult in practice. Without price signals from free markets, it's hard to know what people actually want or need. This often led to shortages of basic goods in communist states.

On freedom: Communist governments have historically been deeply authoritarian. Because the state controls all economic activity, it also controls people's livelihoods, making political dissent very dangerous. The Soviet Union, Maoist China, and North Korea are among the deadliest regimes in human history in terms of their own citizens killed.

On human nature: Critics argue that communism ignores basic human incentives. If your reward is the same regardless of how hard you work, many people will work less. This can reduce overall productivity.

On the state paradox: Communism aims to eliminate the state, but building communism requires a powerful state to manage the transition — and powerful states tend to entrench themselves rather than fade away.

Supporters of communism counter that these failures weren't the result of communism itself, but of the specific conditions in which it was tried — external pressures, war, underdevelopment, and corruption. They argue a genuinely democratic form of communism has never truly been tested.
Different Strands of Communist Thought

Communism is not one single fixed doctrine. Over time, thinkers adapted and argued about it, producing distinct variations:

  • Marxism — The original theoretical framework developed by Marx and Engels.
  • Leninism — Vladimir Lenin's adaptation, which argued that a disciplined, elite revolutionary party must lead the working class to revolution, since workers wouldn't spontaneously organize on their own. This became the basis for Soviet-style communism.
  • Marxism-Leninism — The official ideology of the Soviet Union and most 20th-century communist states. It combined Marx's economic analysis with Lenin's idea of party-led revolution and one-party rule.
  • Maoism — Mao Zedong's adaptation for China, which emphasized the revolutionary potential of the peasantry (farmers) rather than urban factory workers, and added guerrilla warfare strategy.
  • Trotskyism — Leon Trotsky's version, which opposed Stalin's "socialism in one country" and argued for a permanent, international revolution. Trotsky was eventually assassinated on Stalin's orders.
  • Libertarian Communism / Anarcho-Communism — A branch that rejects the idea of a transitional state altogether, arguing that the state itself is the problem and must be abolished immediately along with capitalism, not used as a tool.
Communism Today

As a governing system, communism has largely receded. The Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, and most Eastern European communist states transitioned to capitalist democracies. China and Vietnam retain Communist Parties in power but have embraced market economics to varying degrees. Cuba and North Korea remain ideologically communist states.

As an intellectual tradition, communism and Marxist analysis remain influential in academic and activist circles worldwide. Many thinkers continue to use Marxist frameworks to analyze inequality, labor, and capitalism — even if they don't advocate for the Soviet-style systems of the past.
Summary in One Paragraph

Communism is an ideology that calls for the collective ownership of all productive resources (factories, land, capital), the elimination of social classes, and eventually the dissolution of the state, in order to create a society where goods are distributed based on need rather than profit. It was theorized most influentially by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels in the 19th century as a response to the inequalities of capitalism. In the 20th century, it inspired revolutions in Russia, China, Cuba, and elsewhere, producing powerful but deeply authoritarian states that nationalized economies and suppressed political opposition. These real-world experiments never achieved the classless, stateless ideal Marx described — and most have collapsed or significantly reformed. Today, communism exists more as a living intellectual tradition and a critique of capitalism than as a functioning governing system.
